doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The music business and jazz education
title: Academia, leaving NOCCA, and what makes a good teacher
summary: Jordan resigned from NOCCA (Alvin Batiste replaced him); teachers should keep playing and point students to other information.

venues.name: New Orleans Center for Creative Arts

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I’m curious if you ran into any — even teaching at NOCCA and that kind of thing, did you run into any academia political type things once you get into education?

Well actually yea, I quit NOCCA and now I’m starting like another arts-based school, well I should say, I’m sorry, I resigned. That’s politically more correct. And actually Alvin Batiste took my place when I left NOCCA. And I feel like there’s two things that should happen when you talk about academia. Part of it is that when you get into academia or in a situation where you can teach you should try to practice more and study more and play more. Even though your time is dedicated to obviously teaching. Now the reason why I say that is because you can lose your edge versus even when you’re performing more, you see what I’m saying, you should study more and do those other things just because you’re out there every night maybe on the road or you’re playing a little bit more you lose the edge in terms of the analysis or trying to think about things differently. Just because now it has become playing every night or traveling or whatever it is you’re going to do. So there’s tradeoffs. So in terms of the academia I think the political thing is is that everybody’s trying to figure out what they can offer that may be a little bit differently from the other arts-based type things, you know, if you’re at the high school level. Obviously when you get to the college level it becomes about well if you have a Kenny Barron or if you have a Wynton Marsalis or whoever you have, a Terence Blanchard or whoever you have on your staff as part of your faculty people are attracted to that. But I find, you know, there again, it’s really if you get a great teacher. Somebody who can really teach you your instrument, somebody who can point you in the right direction. If they don’t know the information they say well why don’t you go check out © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

this because I heard this the other night or I read about this or this is something that you may find interesting because you’re interested in this. You know what I mean? To me that’s what’s important. Not that you can think of another class to offer because it sounds good in your course offerings, but to really come up with people who really are knowledgeable. And what I mean by that is where they can point you in the right direction. Because nobody has a monopoly on information. You know what I mean? I mean as great as Berklee School of Music is there are things that’s probably being lost in the cracks that you know they can offer, if they can find somebody or find something where somebody’s doing something a little bit different. And sometimes even at these smaller institutions, like what you guys are doing. I mean I don’t see this happening at Harvard or quote unquote institutions that have jazz degrees. See I’m really, I pick up on all those type of subtleties because we have a tendency to just look at the big picture and not look at what’s really happening.
